title: The science of men
hook: scholars wrote lives of the narrators, to test each one

segments.voice: Yesterday: mutawatir, a report carried by so many chains that it gives certainty.

A story is told about the hadith scholar Ali ibn al-Madini. Someone asked him about a narrator, and the narrator was his own father. He hesitated, and said: ask someone else. They pressed him. And he answered, as the story goes: this is the religion. My father is weak. Whatever the details, the story shows what a whole field of study asked of people: a son choosing accuracy over family pride. Behind that answer stood a library of judgments about people. Today, the science of men.
screen: `ASKED ABOUT HIS OWN FATHER.` → `THIS IS THE RELIGION.` → `A LIBRARY ABOUT PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Rijal means men, and in hadith study it names the narrators themselves, the people in the chains. Despite the word, the books include women who narrated too. Why it began: in the introduction to Sahih Muslim, the early scholar Ibn Sirin is quoted saying, in effect, people didn't use to ask about chains. Then came the time of turmoil, and they said: name your men for us. And again: this knowledge is religion, so look at whom you take your religion from. What the books record: entry after entry, narrator by narrator. Where he lived. Whom he heard from, and who heard from him. Whether he traveled. Was he truthful? Was his memory precise, or did it slip, or fade late in life? Did he write his reports down, and keep the pages safe? The field has a blunt name: al-jarh wa al-ta'dil, wounding and vouching. Each narrator could be wounded by a scholar's criticism, or vouched for. Then a hard question, faced openly. Isn't talking about a man's flaws a kind of backbiting? Imam Muslim answers in that same introduction: exposing a narrator's weakness, to protect what's said in the Prophet's name, isn't forbidden backbiting. It's a duty. Out of this came books of narrators that students of hadith still open. When a scholar grades a report, this is the shelf behind the grade.
screen: `RIJAL: THE PEOPLE IN THE CHAINS.` · `NAME YOUR MEN FOR US.` · `WOUNDING AND VOUCHING.` · `NOT BACKBITING, A DUTY.`

segments.voice: Pick one voice you trust for information, a news outlet, a teacher, a channel, a friend who always knows things, and quietly ask the rijal questions: where do they get what they tell me, have they been wrong and said so, do details drift, do they have a reason to shade the story? You're not putting them on trial, only writing a short entry in your own book of narrators. If you pray, you can ask for fairness in judging.
Rijal. Literally men: the narrators in the chains, and the science of studying who each one was and whether he can be trusted. Today's word.
Your line: who was he? Behind every grade, a shelf of lives. Same time tomorrow.
